title: Is the TI LAUNCHXL-F28P65X the right board for my project?
short: A LaunchPad development kit for TI's TMS320F28P650DK9, a 200 MHz dual-core C28x control chip with 1.28 MB of flash and 248 kB of RAM, almost seven times the RAM of the smaller LAUNCHXL-F2800137. Per cycle, the core behaves exactly like the F2800137's: CoreMark lands at the same 1.294 iterations per MHz from RAM, and the same room-occupancy neural nets pass all 20 test vectors with no source changes. Only one CPU and no CLA have been tried so far; this chip's dual-core side is still untouched.

meet.what: A LaunchPad development kit for TI's TMS320F28P650DK9 control microcontroller, with the XDS110 debug probe built in: one USB cable powers it, flashes it and carries a serial port. Back up the flash before loading the first program if you want the out-of-box factory demo back; no copy of it is saved here.
facts: Dual-core C28x at 200 MHz, each core with its own CLA (control law accelerator). Not Arm. Only CPU1 has run; CPU2 and both CLAs are not used
CAN-FD, SCI (TI's UART), SPI, FSI, EtherCAT, two eQEP encoder inputs, 12-bit and 16-bit ADC headers; no camera interface, no video hardware

XDS110, on the board. Debug link is 4-pin JTAG by default; probe firmware 3.0.0.43 for CCStudio 21.0.1. A hand-written connection file needs a line this chip's dual-core, CLA-equipped design adds (see the FAQ)
Two 80-pin BoosterPack XL sites, a 12-bit/16-bit differential ADC header, two eQEP connectors, an FSI connector, a CAN connector, EtherCAT RJ45 connectors
TI C2000Ware and the C2000 compiler; TI Arm tools do not apply

projects.t: Blink an LED with TI's SDK
projects.result: TI's `led_ex1_blinky` built in 8.6 s from a terminal and was written to flash; the LED pin (GPIO12, LED4) toggled every 500 ms, confirmed by eye. Box to blink: not stopwatched end to end

Same model source as the LAUNCHXL-F2800137 and the MSPM0 boards, ported with no source changes: 0.893 / 2.365 / 8.380 / 47.907 ms per inference, 20 of 20 test vectors right in every build, faster in wall-clock time than the F2800137's own figures at every size. The 30k model's 67 kB of weights did not fit this session's RAM layout and ran from flash instead; not a chip-capacity limit (248 kB total RAM against the F2800137's 36 kB), a linker-layout one we did not chase further

Unmodified it does not validate (16-bit byte, same as every C28x). With the same three-change patch used on the F2800137, every check matches the standard run: 211.79 per second (1.059 per MHz) from flash, 258.86 (1.294 per MHz) from RAM, an exact match to the F2800137's own RAM figure. Unofficial

Unmodified source (the same files used on the MSPM0 boards), rules followed (-O3, no automatic inlining): 0.444 DMIPS per MHz from RAM, 0.279 from flash, matching the F2800137's own 0.442 almost exactly

1.56 cycles per register write, clock-independent, identical to the F2800137. Interrupt latency through the PIE: 30 cycles from RAM, 36 from flash, zero jitter, matching the F2800137's own 30-cycle figure. Porting the F2800137's own test here first failed silently (0 samples) because this chip's INT_FREERTOS line is PIE 12.12, not 12.6 like the F2800137; see the FAQ

Clean to 12.5 Mbaud (200 MHz divided by 16, the SCI's hardware ceiling at this clock) using the SCI's own internal loopback, zero errors across all 20 speeds tried. A true wire loop, like the one run on the F2800137, still needs a jumper on the SCI pins and has not been tried

chains.t: TI C2000Ware and compiler, from a terminal
chains.why: A build script retargets TI's SysConfig output to the LAUNCHXL-F28P65X and the exact TMS320F28P650DK9 part. SysConfig otherwise defaults to a different C2000 board and chip variant. The script then compiles, links and loads with the same scripting runner used on the F2800137

chains.t: A connection file built the way the F2800137's was
chains.why: Fails every operation, including a plain probe identify, with "An invalid processor ID has been found": this chip's dual-core, CLA-equipped design needs a driver line and a narrower connection the single-core template never carried. Start from TI's own targetConfigs file for this chip instead

2 wait states with prefetch and cache cost 18 to 37% more cycles than RAM, depending on the program. CoreMark costs 18% and Dhrystone 37%, a bigger hit than on the F2800137, where the same two tests cost 10 to 22%

chains.t: A radio or wireless connectivity demo
chains.why: This chip has no radio hardware: CAN-FD, SPI, SCI, FSI and EtherCAT only. The BLE, Zigbee and Thread demos that run on TI's radio boards (the LP-EM-CC2340R5 and LP-CC1354P10-1) need silicon this chip does not have

combine_lede: Checked against the vendor's documentation before anything was tried on the bench.
benchmarks: SCI internal loopback, fastest clean speed
Did not fit the RAM layout built
glance: Patched for the 16-bit byte, unofficial, from RAM; an exact match to the LAUNCHXL-F2800137's own figure
Almost seven times the F2800137's 36 kB; the largest room-occupancy model still needed a wider linker layout than the one built
200 MHz divided by 16, the SCI's hardware ceiling at this clock; zero errors in internal loopback
Zero jitter; matches the F2800137's own RAM figure once the chip's own interrupt-line number is used
500 weights, plain C, 20 of 20 right; faster than the same model on the F2800137
Dual-core C28x, each with its own CLA; neither the second CPU nor either CLA has been used yet
good_for: Anyone already comfortable with the LAUNCHXL-F2800137 who needs more RAM or flash: the core behaves exactly the same per cycle, so existing C2000 code and knowledge carries straight over
Big buffers and bigger neural nets: 248 kB of RAM fit every room-occupancy model we tried without needing flash, except where our linker layout ran out of contiguous room first
Building and running from a Mac terminal with TI's own tools, the same workflow proven on the F2800137
not_for: Anything with a radio: this chip has no wireless hardware at all, only CAN-FD, SPI, SCI, FSI and EtherCAT
Video decode of any kind: no camera interface, no video DMA, no codec hardware
A first C2000 board if you want the cheapest start: the LAUNCHXL-F28P55X ($31.90) is less expensive, and the LAUNCHXL-F2800137 ($35.09) has the fuller test history so far
Projects that need the dual-core or CLA story proven today: both are present on this chip but untouched by any test run so far
buy: US$47.19 on TI.com (ti.com/tool/LAUNCHXL-F28P65X, read 2026-10-08). The debug probe is on the board, so one USB cable does power, flashing and the serial port.
gotchas: A hand-written connection file fails every operation with "An invalid processor ID has been found"

This chip's dual-core, CLA-equipped design needs a driver line and a narrower connection a single-core board's template does not carry. Start from TI's own `targetConfigs/TMS320F28P650DK9.ccxml` in C2000Ware instead. **Tag: Tool or docs.**
A test ported from another C2000 chip runs with no error but never measures anything

If the test pends an interrupt by writing a specific bit number, reread this chip's own `hw_ints.h` first. The same interrupt can sit on a different PIE line on a different C2000 chip, and no compiler error catches the mismatch. **Tag: Chip limit.**
measured_on: Measured 2026-10-08 on an Intel Mac (macOS 15.7.9) with CCStudio 21.0.1, C2000 compiler 25.11.1.LTS and C2000Ware 26.02.00.00 LTS. Code from RAM and from flash (2 wait states), 200 MHz.

next.title: What do I do first with the LAUNCHXL-F28P65X?
steps: If the probe's firmware is below 3.0.0.43, update it with TI's `xdsdfu`, the same tool and steps as the LAUNCHXL-F2800137
Build a connection file from C2000Ware's own `device_support/f28p65x/common/targetConfigs/TMS320F28P650DK9.ccxml`, not from a single-core board's file; add only the probe's serial number
Build and load TI's `led_ex1_blinky` from a terminal: `c2000-launchpad/tools/c2kbuild_f28p65x.sh <folder> FLASH`, then the scripting runner `c2000-launchpad/tools/c2krun_f28p65x.js`
Read this board's FAQ for the two problems specific to this chip, and the LAUNCHXL-F2800137's FAQ for problems common to C2000 LaunchPad development kits in general

line: Two cores, each with a control law accelerator, plus EtherCAT and CAN-FD. Only the first core has run.
